record.title: Anthropic releases FlashProve, a zero-knowledge proof prototype for model inference
record.summary: Anthropic released FlashProve, an open-source prototype for proving that an inference response matches a commitment to a model’s weights. It reports performance for a 4-bit Llama 4 Maverick model, with substantial proving overhead and a CPU-verifiable proof. Its linked technical report says it was AI-generated and not reviewed in detail; it also says batched zero-knowledge is not proved, executable C++ equivalence to Lean is unproved, and the verified statement concerns an integer-quantized model’s greedy output. The results remain first-party prototype claims, not independent validation or production evidence.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Anthropic published a Nov 2, 2026 research post announcing FlashProve, an open-source prototype for zero-knowledge provable inference, with a technical report, protocol description, executable prover and verifiers, and Lean proof artifacts described as released under Apache 2.0.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Anthropic reports that FlashProve generates inference proofs for 4-bit quantized Llama 4 Maverick, a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, at about 110 tokens per second on one H100 GPU, with proof size around 19 MB per 1,024-token request and GPU time about 70–95 times the vLLM inference time for prompts of the same length.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Anthropic says the proof binds an inference response to a commitment to particular model weights, while hiding those weights; it does not aim to hide the model architecture.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The public announcement does not establish independent replication, production serving performance, end-to-end operational security, or that proof of inference alone can show a provider is not also using hardware for training.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The public anthropics/FlashProve GitHub repository identifies version 0.16.0 as a research artifact that is not maintained and is not accepting contributions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The repository README lists full Llama 4 Maverick proof generation as requiring a single NVIDIA H100 80 GB, CUDA 13.2, 330 GB RAM, 245 GB disk and hours of execution; its stored-proof verifier route is listed separately as requiring under 2 GB RAM.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Anthropic’s technical report says it was AI-generated and had not been reviewed in detail.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The report says the Lean formalization proves zero-knowledge only when requests are processed one at a time, not in batches, and that the executable C++ code is not formally proved equivalent to the Lean specification.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The reported protocol does not establish proof coverage for ordinary floating-point or sampled production replies; it proves an integer-quantized model’s greedy choice, and post-hoc proof generation detects a mismatch after the response rather than preventing delivery of an initially tampered response.

evidence_gaps.description: Performance, proof validity and security are reported by the project authors; no independent benchmark or cryptographic audit was inspected.

The announcement explicitly says proof that hardware serves inference does not establish the absence of simultaneous training; production throughput, verification time, service overhead and scaling remain unestablished.

The technical report was inspected but says it was AI-generated and not reviewed in detail. The repository’s protocol source, GPU prover, C++ verifier and Lean theorem implementation have not been audited; the report explicitly says executable C++ equivalence to Lean is unproved and zero-knowledge for batched requests is not proved.

brief.importance_rationale: If practical beyond the reported prototype, proofs tied to specific model weights could let users, evaluators and regulators verify which model produced an inference response without learning its weights. That could improve model-integrity auditing and some policy checks. The release is intermediate research; its performance and security claims remain first-party and the reported overhead is high relative to ordinary inference.
limitations: Performance and cryptographic-security statements are first-party claims in the inspected official post.
The reported regime is specific to a single H100 and 4-bit Llama 4 Maverick; it does not establish general performance across architectures, hardware or quantization formats.
The cited 70–95x comparison indicates substantial proof-generation cost relative to ordinary vLLM inference.
Anthropic explicitly notes that proof of serving inference does not establish that the same hardware is not also training.
The official repository labels FlashProve version 0.16.0 a research artifact that is not maintained and is not accepting contributions.

The repository README lists full-size Llama 4 Maverick proving as requiring one H100 80 GB, CUDA 13.2, 330 GB RAM and 245 GB disk, with execution measured in hours; these are documented requirements, not independently tested here.
Anthropic’s technical report says it was AI-generated and not reviewed in detail; its technical analysis therefore remains first-party provisional material.
The report says formal zero-knowledge is proved for one-at-a-time requests, not batch proving, and the executable C++ code is not proved equivalent to the Lean specification.
The measured claim concerns the integer-quantized model and greedy-choice token, not exact equivalence to ordinary floating-point or sampled production responses.
Proofs are generated post-hoc: they can detect tampering after a reply is delivered, but cannot prevent the initial delivery of a tampered reply; the report treats this as defense in depth.
brief.summary: Anthropic released FlashProve, an open-source prototype for proving that an inference response matches a commitment to a model’s weights. It reports performance for a 4-bit Llama 4 Maverick model, with substantial proving overhead and a CPU-verifiable proof. Its linked technical report says it was AI-generated and not reviewed in detail; it also says batched zero-knowledge is not proved, executable C++ equivalence to Lean is unproved, and the verified statement concerns an integer-quantized model’s greedy output. The results remain first-party prototype claims, not independent validation or production evidence.

technical.claimed_result: Anthropic reports about 110 proof tokens/s on one H100 for 4-bit Llama 4 Maverick (400B parameters), approximately 19 MB per 1,024-token request, and 70–95x vLLM inference GPU time.
technical.demonstrated_result: Anthropic publicly announced the FlashProve prototype and described associated report, protocol, prover, C++ verifier and Lean artifacts. The artifacts and benchmark were not independently executed in this review.
technical.implementation_status: Public intermediate research prototype. The linked official GitHub repository identifies version 0.16.0 as not maintained and not accepting contributions.
technical.mechanism: A prover commits to model weights and produces a zero-knowledge succinct proof associated with an inference response; a verifier checks the proof without receiving the weights.
technical.regime: Anthropic reports a single H100; 4-bit quantized Llama 4 Maverick MoE; integer arithmetic in prefill; and 1,024-token request proof-size comparison. The repository README lists full-model route requirements of an H100 80 GB, CUDA 13.2, 330 GB RAM and 245 GB disk.
technical.reproducibility: The official report was retrieved and inspected, but it says it was AI-generated and not reviewed in detail. The repository is marked an unmaintained research artifact. Neither implementation nor Lean proofs were audited or run independently; C++ equivalence to the Lean specification is unproved, and formal zero-knowledge coverage does not yet extend to batched requests.
technical.strongest_baseline: Anthropic compares proof-generation GPU time with vLLM inference GPU time for prompts of the same length; the post does not establish an independent matched performance study.

brief.title: Anthropic releases FlashProve, a zero-knowledge proof prototype for model inference
brief.why_it_matters: Provable inference could give users and auditors a cryptographic way to check model identity across hosted or routed services, and could support some compliance checks. FlashProve offers a public prototype and formal-verification artifacts, but the reported compute cost is substantial, the linked artifacts were not audited here, and proof of inference does not rule out simultaneous training or settle broader compliance.
